6607-myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-v:
Dolph Heyliger, a graceless but brave New York lad, opens the second volume, set on the Isle of Manhattoes and nearby shores. Left poor when his father dies, Dolph takes service with a doctor who owns a farm out where Twenty-third Street now runs. Rumors about the place, and tenants who whisper of it, soon pull him into trouble.

Other tales in the volume follow: a knell at a wedding, roistering Dutchmen, a party from Gibbet Island, and the devil's stepping-stones. Skinner keeps the old New Amsterdam flavor, with Dutch names and harbor lore. This volume is a charming, ghostly tour of early New York and its near waters.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AtzenhofferAnth:
On January 24, 1964, FBI agents in Dallas interviewed Anthony 'Tony' Atzenhoffer Jr. as part of the Kennedy assassination investigation. Atzenhoffer had been a cadet in the Civil Air Patrol, and the Bureau wanted his memory of a fellow cadet from years before: Lee Harvey Oswald.

The interview report records his recollection that Oswald had been in the Civil Air Patrol in New Orleans. The cadet squadron there was once commanded by David Ferrie, a figure who later drew investigators' attention. Single interview reports like this one are the bricks of the FBI's Oswald file, each testing one small claim against a witness.
myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-volume:
Charles M. Skinner devotes this volume to Manhattan and lands nearby. Dolph Heyliger opens the tales in old New Amsterdam. Dolph was a brave, penniless scamp left by his father's death. He took service with a doctor who owned a haunted farm.

Rumors kept tenants off that farm, up where Twenty-third Street now runs. Dolph was sent to spend three nights in the lone manor. He came out pale but kept his counsel, to the town's rage. Wedding knells, devil's stepping-stones, and bloody springs fill the contents. Skinner finds thick folklore under the modern city's streets and farms.
